body: Three winters ago, frightened, a man bought a stack of tins, and at half past five on a Saturday morning he is standing in a cold lock-up with a torch, going through them. Chopped tomatoes, mostly. Some soup. He turns each one to find the date and puts it in one of two carrier bags at his feet, and by the time the light comes up the bag on the left is nearly empty and the bag on the right has split under the weight. He carries it out to the car in two goes and does not say anything to his wife about where he is taking it.
It was not really about tomatoes. What he had bought, three winters ago, was the feeling of not having to think about it any more, and what he was carrying out to the car was that feeling, expired.

The manna arrangement is one of the odder logistical setups in the text. Enough for one day, gathered every morning, and anything kept overnight went off — with a single exception before the Sabbath, which is what shows the spoiling was a rule rather than a property of the substance.

It is worth taking the word daily literally rather than reading past it. This was not a gift; it was an issue schedule, and the schedule was the message. There was no market in the wilderness and nowhere to put anything by, so the whole camp was placed on a ration that had to be collected before the sun got at it. Every household got up. Every household went out. The supply was never in question after the first week, and that is precisely the point people miss: the supply was reliable and the reserve was forbidden. God did not withdraw the bread. He withdrew the ability to stop thinking about where it came from.

This band has a frequency set aside for the subject. HM 381.80 — The Hidden Manna — is assigned and in build, not yet on air, still silent. The dial itself runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are playing right now, which is the only tense a broadcast has.

That is a hard arrangement to be under and the text does not pretend otherwise. They were given exactly one day’s worth, and what they hoarded bred worms — and the detail about worms is the kind of thing that survives because somebody was there and never quite got over it. It is not a parable about greed. Nobody in that camp was getting rich on stored bread. They were doing what any sensible person does, which is to put a little aside so that tomorrow is settled, and the arrangement would not let them, and it kept not letting them for forty years.

That has become an almost incomprehensible way to live, because everything now is a store. The subscription is a store, the saved library is a store, the downloaded seasons and the read-later queue are stores too. None of it is wicked and most of it is convenient. But it has trained a whole culture to relate to good things as inventory — to acquire access rather than to receive anything — and a person who has acquired access to more music than they can hear in a lifetime is not thereby a person who has listened to any of it. The stockpile grows and the day stays empty.

Look at how the band is arranged and it runs the other way. Every station holds one frequency permanently, the schedule is published before it airs, and what is playing at ten past four is what is playing at ten past four. You cannot get ahead of it. Two people who tune to the same number at the same second hear the same song, and neither of them can bank the one after it against a worse afternoon.
There is a serious objection to all of this, and it is not a pious one. Scripture itself keeps praising the people who store.

The ant is commended for gathering in summer. Joseph filled the granaries of Egypt for seven years and the whole region ate because of it, and the man who leaves his family with nothing is called worse than an unbeliever. So prudence is not the enemy here and nobody should read the manna and cancel the pension. But look at what those stores are actually for. The ant feeds a winter. Joseph fed nations, including the brothers who sold him. Both of those are stores kept on behalf of somebody else, at a cost to the person keeping them. The hoard in the wilderness was kept on behalf of the hoarder, and the only thing it was ever going to buy was the end of a daily conversation.
And nothing that actually keeps a person alive keeps.

It is twenty to four in the morning and a woman is standing in a hallway with a baby against her shoulder, moving from foot to foot because it is the only thing that works. The boiler ticks. There is a light on in the kitchen behind her that she cannot be bothered to go and turn off. For the first fortnight she did the arithmetic every night — if he goes down now that is five hours, if he wakes at six that is three and a half — and at some point in the second month she stopped doing it, because the number was never right and knowing it never helped. Now she works to the next feed and no further. She could not tell you when she gave up on the week as a unit. She only knows she is less tired since she did.

Nothing about her situation improved. What changed is that she stopped trying to hold a supply she was never going to be issued, and the exhaustion of guarding a reserve that did not exist came off the top of the day.

None of which is a comfortable doctrine, and it should not be presented as one. Living without a reserve means daily dependence, and daily dependence is not a serene feeling. It means you cannot get ahead, cannot bank a good week against a bad one, cannot arrive at Friday with anything in hand. Anybody who tells you this arrangement is peaceful has probably not been under it. It is a wearing way to live and the wearing part is the part that does not go away.

But that is not a defect in the arrangement. It is the arrangement. A reserve does one thing above all others: it lets you stop asking. The household with a fortnight of bread in the tent does not go out in the morning, and the family that goes out in the morning is the family that has to keep noticing where the bread comes from. The strain of having no store is the strain of a relationship that gets renewed rather than settled, and the settled version — the one where the account is topped up and nobody has to speak — was never on offer.

So the pattern holds for nearly everything that sustains a person. Prayer does not accumulate into a balance that covers a dry month. Neither does forgiveness, or attention, or the plain energy required to be decent to your own family at the end of a bad day. All of it is issued daily, none of it stores, and the arrangement is deliberate rather than a design fault. Whatever is worth having tomorrow will be given tomorrow, and it will be given to somebody who turns up for it.
All of which is theory until there is a Tuesday to get through. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming and it is worth knowing they are there. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, gospel, hymns, country. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe: entertaining, clean, and playable in a room with children in it whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards. Four kinds, one dial, and no menu to work through to reach them.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 301.90 — Radiant Stones Concerts. Of everything on this dial it is the least storable thing on it, and that is exactly why it belongs to this argument. A concert is one room on one night. The people in it did not get to keep it and could not have gathered a second night against a worse one; they got what was given while they were standing there, and everything else about that evening is gone. Put it on and you are in the same position they were. You will not have chosen the running order, you cannot skip to the part you would have wanted, and whatever is playing when you arrive is your portion of it. That is not a limitation of the format. It is the format telling the truth about how most good things arrive.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for, which is how the next station gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not save it for later; later is exactly the thing this article has been arguing does not work. Put HM 301.90 on this afternoon, while the washing is going round and there is nothing much on, and take what is on when you get there. It is one day’s worth. That has always been the size of the ration, and it has always been enough for the day it was issued for.
